intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with hypotonia, language delay, and skeletal defects with or without seizures (NEDHLSS) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the CACNA1C gene (114205) on chromosome 12p13.

checks.claim: Neurodevelopmental disorder with hypotonia, language delay, and skeletal defects with or without seizures (NEDHLSS) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the CACNA1C gene.
checks.evidence_quote: We describe the clinical and molecular details of 3 individuals from 2 unrelated families with heterozygous variants in CACNA1C.
checks.explanation: The paper reports heterozygous CACNA1C variants in patients with epilepsy, hypotonia and developmental delay. It frames them as Timothy syndrome-like or expanded CACNA1C-related disorders and never names the NEDHLSS entity.

checks.claim: The CACNA1C gene is located on chromosome 12p13.
checks.evidence_quote: caused by heterozygous mutations in CACNA1C, a gene encoding a calcium channel
checks.explanation: The chromosomal location is standard nomenclature added to the gene named in the paper.

paragraphs.text: NEDHLSS is a CACNA1C-related neurologic disorder with variable developmental delay, intellectual disability, autism, epilepsy, hypotonia, and ataxia (Rodan et al., 2021). Many patients also have orthopedic abnormalities such as clubfoot, hip dysplasia, syndactyly, and joint hypermobility. Unlike in Timothy syndrome, significant cardiac abnormalities and the classic Timothy syndrome features are usually absent.

checks.claim: NEDHLSS is a CACNA1C-related neurologic disorder with variable developmental delay, intellectual disability, autism, epilepsy, hypotonia, and ataxia.
checks.evidence_quote: we delineate the phenotypic spectrum of a CACNA1C-related neurological disorder variably associated with developmental delay, intellectual disability, autism, epilepsy, hypotonia, and ataxia.

paragraphs.text: Bozarth et al. (2018) reported a girl (patient 1) of English maternal and Ukrainian paternal ancestry born to nonconsanguineous, unaffected parents. Her seizures began within a few hours of birth, with numerous subtle tonic seizures and prolonged tonic and tonic-myoclonic seizures every day. She also had epileptic tonic spasms and focal seizures with eye blinking and facial twitching. Her epileptic encephalopathy was drug-resistant, and EEG showed diffuse excessive fast activity. She had profound axial and appendicular hypotonia, made no developmental progress, and could not visually track or fixate. Other findings included neonatal hypoglycemia, short length at birth, laryngomalacia with stridor, bilateral clubfeet, bilateral 3-4 finger and 2-3 toe syndactyly, camptodactyly, micrognathia, downturned corners of the mouth, frontal bossing, very scant hair, inverted nipples, and mild optic nerve hypoplasia. She had severe gastroesophageal reflux, constipation, anal stenosis, and severe dysphagia requiring gastrostomy, as well as a disturbed sleep-wake cycle and central and obstructive sleep apnea. Brain MRI, echocardiogram, and Holter monitoring were normal. She was last reported at 18 months of age. The authors noted that she had many hallmark features of Timothy syndrome, including cutaneous syndactyly, dysmorphic features, and sleep disturbance, but no cardiac abnormalities. She differed from previously reported individuals in having severe refractory neonatal-onset epilepsy, no neurodevelopmental progress, and a recognizable EEG pattern of diffuse fast activity.

paragraphs.text: Bozarth et al. (2018) also reported a nonconsanguineous family of Irish and German ancestry. The proband (patient 2), a girl, had tetralogy of Fallot that was surgically repaired at 2 months of age. She also had left ventricular noncompaction and acute severe biventricular failure. She had mild developmental delay at 8 months, and by 12 months she spoke 10 words and first walked. Neurologic examination showed mild diffuse hypotonia. She had a flat nasal bridge, low-set ears, cupped superior helices, deep-set eyes with shallow orbits, a thin vermilion border of the upper lip, a round face, and mild bilateral 2-3-4 toe syndactyly. Her father (patient 3) had a congenital ventricular septal defect and aortic valve stenosis, repaired at 2.5 months of age. He had learning disabilities requiring an individualized education program and attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and by 18 years he had developed focal to bilateral tonic-clonic seizures. His craniofacial features resembled his daughter's: low-set ears, a thin upper lip vermilion, premaxillary underdevelopment, and a round face.

paragraphs.text: Rodan et al. (2021) reported 25 individuals from 22 families with heterozygous CACNA1C variants. Significant cardiac abnormalities and classic Timothy syndrome features were absent in all but one; that patient (P13) had a prolonged QT interval. All 14 individuals with de novo nontruncating variants had developmental delay or intellectual disability. Nine of the 14 were nonverbal, 12 had hypotonia, and 10 had epilepsy, with onset between 2 months and 8 years of age. Twelve had orthopedic abnormalities, including clubfoot, hip dysplasia, syndactyly, and joint hypermobility. Seizure types included: - absence and generalized tonic-clonic seizures (P1) - fever-sensitive focal motor and absence seizures (P2) - focal seizures (P3) - West syndrome/infantile spasms (P6) - myoclonic and generalized tonic-clonic seizures (P7) - fever-sensitive generalized epilepsy (P8) - behavioral arrest spells with or without head or limb jerking (P9) - febrile seizures (P11) - myoclonic seizures evolving to generalized epilepsy (P12) - infantile spasms evolving to Lennox-Gastaut syndrome (P13) - generalized epilepsy beginning at 2 months (P14) P4, P5, and P10 had no seizures. Movement abnormalities included action tremor of the arms that resolved (P4), intention tremor of the arms with head tremor and ataxia (P5), and leg spasticity (P10). Several patients were nonambulatory. Skeletal findings were: - pes planovalgus (P1, P5) - congenital hip dysplasia (P2, P14) - hip dislocation and subluxation (P4) - joint hypermobility (P3, P4, P5) - bilateral clubfoot with adducted thumbs (P7, P10), with camptodactyly in P10 - kyphosis (P8) - tapered fingers and small-appearing feet (P9) - 2-3 toe and 3-4 finger syndactyly with congenital torticollis (P11) - kyphoscoliosis and coxa valga (P12) - 2-3 toe syndactyly and bilateral adducted thumbs (P14) Ocular findings included strabismus, hyperopia, myopia, esotropia, and cortical visual impairment. P4 had a small interatrial communication with left-to-right shunt, and P12 had a possible ventricular conduction delay.

paragraphs.text: Rodan et al. (2021) also described 11 individuals from 8 families with truncating CACNA1C variants, whose deficits were milder and more selective.
